payload_or_id.description: The only client-facing operation: api.get_value(cache, key). Delegates straight to Cache.get and returns whatever it gets. Instrumented with a single Prometheus counter kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome=success|error}; the error label is incremented only on StorageError, which propagates to the caller. Correctness of the returned value is invisible here -- a cache hit returns the cached value whether it is fresh or stale, and the counter records success either way.

Internal, non-client-facing write entrypoint: admin.update_value(storage, cache, key, value). Not reachable from external clients. Writes through to Storage.put only; it takes a Cache parameter but never calls cache.evict(key), so a cached reader keeps the pre-write value. Entirely uninstrumented -- no counter, no latency, no error metric.

In-process, in-memory cache (cache.Cache) sitting in front of Storage, holding key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms). Cache.get consults its own dict first and only falls back to storage on a miss; it never re-checks storage for an already-cached key and never expires anything itself. Negative lookups are cached too (value=None is stored as an entry). Expiry and size bounding are delegated entirely to the eviction pass. Uninstrumented: no hit/miss counter, no entry-count gauge, no age distribution.

Backing key-value store (storage.Storage): a single delimited flat text file, one 'key,value' pair per line, read and rewritten in full on every operation. get() scans every line and returns the first key match, or None if the file is absent or the key is not found. put() reads the whole file into a dict, sets the key, mkdir -p's the parent, and rewrites the whole file. OSError is wrapped as StorageError; no other failure is signalled. Uninstrumented: no operation counter, no latency, no file-size or line-count metric.

The local filesystem and the flat file path Storage was constructed with. Supplies durability, capacity, and permissions for every read and write. Its failures surface only as OSError -> StorageError; its capacity, free space, and the file's growth are not observed by anything in the service.

evictor.run_eviction_pass(cache): walks every entry via Cache.items(), evicts those older than TTL_SECONDS (300), and returns the number removed so a caller could log progress. This is the only mechanism that bounds cache size or expires stale entries. It compares a seconds-based `now` against Entry.inserted_at_ms (milliseconds), so the expiry condition is never true and the returned count is always 0. The return value is the only observability signal it offers, and nothing in the repo consumes it.

The out-of-repo scheduler/loop that is expected to invoke run_eviction_pass on an interval. No code in this repo calls it, configures its period, or records that a pass ran, so whether eviction executes at all is unobservable from inside the service.

The out-of-repo periodic data-sync job named as the caller of admin.update_value. It is the only writer of new values into storage. Its schedule, success, and volume of writes are defined outside this repo and are not recorded by any metric in it, so a sync that stops running, or one that writes bad values, is invisible to the service.

prometheus_client 0.26.0 and the scrape path that reads its default registry. Holds the service's one metric, kvstore_get_value_requests_total. No HTTP exposition endpoint (start_http_server or equivalent) is created anywhere in this repo, so the registry has no confirmed sink -- every metric added later depends on this gap being closed to be alertable at all.

event.text:
Phase 1 accepted — 9 `system_components` entries recorded.

**The service.** `kvstore` is a read-mostly key-value store: one client-facing read (`api.get_value`), an in-memory cache in front of a flat-file store, a background TTL eviction pass, and an internal write path used by an out-of-repo sync job.

**Map as recorded** (arrows = `depends_on`):

```
sm-data-sync-job ──▶ sm-admin-update-value ──▶ sm-storage-layer ──▶ sm-backing-file-fs
sm-api-get-value ──▶ sm-cache-layer ────────▶ sm-storage-layer
       └──────────▶ sm-prometheus-registry
sm-eviction-scheduler ──▶ sm-eviction-pass ──▶ sm-cache-layer
```

**Choices worth flagging before Phase 2:**

- **Two out-of-repo callers are modelled as components** (`sm-eviction-scheduler`, `sm-data-sync-job`) rather than left implicit. Both are upstream links in real failure chains: if the scheduler never fires, or the sync job stops writing, nothing inside the service records it. Making them components lets Phase 2 attach failure modes to them directly.
- **The filesystem is separated from the storage layer.** Capacity and permission failures belong to the filesystem; the full-file rewrite pattern belongs to `storage.py`. They fail differently and want different detection.
- **The Prometheus registry is a dependency with a gap already noted.** No exposition endpoint exists anywhere in the repo — no `start_http_server`, no ASGI mount. Every metric I recommend in Phase 3 is unalertable until that is confirmed, so I recorded it now rather than discovering it at Phase 4.

**Instrumentation baseline:** exactly one metric exists, `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`, and it only distinguishes "raised `StorageError`" from "returned". A stale value, a cache miss, an unbounded cache, and a key collision all increment `outcome="success"`. The cache, storage, evictor, and write path have no instrumentation at all.

Three things I noted in the source that will drive Phase 2, all several hops upstream of anything a user would see:

1. `evictor.py` compares a seconds-valued `now` against a millisecond-valued `inserted_at_ms`, so the expiry condition is never true — nothing is ever evicted and the returned count is permanently 0.
2. `admin.update_value` takes a `Cache` argument and never calls `cache.evict(key)`, so writes never invalidate cached reads.
3. `storage.get` splits on the first comma and returns the first key match, so a key or value containing a comma can collide or truncate silently.

The run pauses here for your review. Say when to start Phase 2 (failure modes).

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
Phase 1's map gives me the chains. Now enumerating failure modes, upstream links first.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass never expires anything (seconds vs milliseconds)
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.get sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS. The expired list is always empty, no entry is ever evicted, and the function always returns 0. The pass can run perfectly on schedule and still do nothing -- the only in-code signal it offers (the return count) reads identically to a healthy idle cache.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: No code in this repo calls run_eviction_pass; the scheduler that is supposed to drive it lives outside the service. If it is never wired up, is misconfigured, crashes, or has its interval set far longer than TTL_SECONDS, eviction simply does not happen. This is independent of fm-evictor-unit-mismatch and produces the same downstream effects, so fixing the unit bug alone does not close the chain.

payload_or_id.name: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value accepts a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put; it never calls cache.evict(key). Cache.get never re-checks storage for a key it already holds, so the cache and the backing store diverge the instant a write lands for any cached key. The divergence persists until eviction removes the entry -- which, given fm-evictor-unit-mismatch and fm-eviction-not-scheduled, is never.

payload_or_id.name: Missing-key result is cached as a permanent negative
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the storage result unconditionally, including None for a key that does not yet exist, and its hit check is `entry is not None` on the Entry rather than on the value. A key read before it is first written is pinned to None in the cache. Combined with the broken eviction, that negative is permanent for the process lifetime, so the key stays invisible no matter how many times it is later written.

payload_or_id.name: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get inserts an entry for every key it is asked about and nothing removes entries, so resident set grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Under sustained unique-key traffic -- including a scan, a scraper, or an attacker requesting random keys -- growth is bounded only by available memory. Nothing in the service reports the entry count, so the growth is invisible until the process dies.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file grows without bound and is rescanned in full
payload_or_id.description: Storage has no delete operation and put rewrites the entire file, so the file only ever grows. Every get does a full read_text plus a linear scan, and every put does a full read plus a full rewrite, making both O(file size). Cost per operation therefore rises continuously with key count. No metric records file size, line count, or operation latency.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file cannot be read
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get wraps OSError as StorageError: the file exists but is unreadable through lost permissions, a corrupt or unmounted filesystem, an exhausted file-descriptor limit, or an I/O error. Note the asymmetry -- an absent file is NOT an error here, it returns None, so a lost or wiped store reads as 'every key missing' rather than as a failure.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file cannot be written
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put wraps OSError as StorageError: disk full, read-only remount, lost permissions, or a failed parent mkdir. StorageError propagates to admin.update_value, which neither catches nor records it, and on to the out-of-repo sync job whose handling is unknown. Reads keep succeeding from the stale file throughout, so the service looks entirely healthy while it has stopped accepting new data.

payload_or_id.name: Filesystem full, unmounted, or permission-changed
payload_or_id.description: The volume holding the store file fills, is remounted read-only, is unmounted, or has its ownership changed. This is the shared root cause beneath both storage read and write failures and beneath the non-atomic rewrite hazard. Free space and mount state are external conditions that the service never samples, and they are detectable well before any operation actually fails.

payload_or_id.name: Whole-store rewrite is not atomic
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads every pair into a dict and then calls write_text on the live path, truncating the real file and rewriting it in place with no temp-file-and-rename. A crash, OOM kill, container eviction, or ENOSPC part-way through the write leaves the store truncated or half-written -- every key after the truncation point is destroyed, not just the one being written. The blast radius of one failed write is the entire dataset.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file with no lock and no compare-and-swap. Two overlapping puts each read the pre-existing state and the later writer's rewrite discards the earlier writer's key. A concurrent get can also observe the file mid-rewrite and read a truncated snapshot. Both puts return successfully, so the loss is entirely silent.

payload_or_id.name: Key containing the delimiter collides with another key
payload_or_id.description: Lines are split with partition(','), taking everything before the first comma as the key. A stored key containing a comma -- 'a,b' with value 'v' -- is written as the line 'a,b,v', which on read parses as key 'a' with value 'b,v'. A lookup of the unrelated key 'a' matches that line and returns 'b,v'. The store has no escaping or quoting, so key namespaces that permit commas silently alias onto each other.

payload_or_id.name: Newline in a value corrupts subsequent records
payload_or_id.description: Records are separated by newlines with no escaping, so a value containing a newline is written as two physical lines. On the next read the tail of that value is parsed as an independent record whose key is whatever precedes its first comma, injecting a phantom key and a corrupt value into the store. A single write of untrusted content can therefore create or overwrite arbitrary keys.

payload_or_id.name: Data-sync job stops running
payload_or_id.description: The out-of-repo periodic sync job is the only writer of new values. If it stops being scheduled, crashes, or fails every run against StorageError, the store simply stops receiving updates. Every read keeps succeeding and returning the last-synced value, so the service's one existing metric stays entirely green while the data it serves ages without limit.

payload_or_id.name: No metrics exposition endpoint exists
payload_or_id.description: The package creates a Counter but never starts an exposition endpoint (no start_http_server, no ASGI/WSGI mount, no pushgateway call) anywhere in the repo. If the embedding process does not provide one, kvstore_get_value_requests_total is incremented into a registry nothing ever reads. Every alert recommended in phase 4 depends on this being closed first -- an unscraped metric is indistinguishable from a healthy silent one.

payload_or_id.name: Metrics stop being scraped while the service runs
payload_or_id.description: The scrape path breaks in production -- endpoint down, target dropped from service discovery, network partition to Prometheus -- while the service keeps serving. Every alert built on these metrics goes blind simultaneously, and absence-of-data reads the same as absence-of-problems for any rate-threshold rule. This is the failure that silently disables detection of every other failure here, which is why it pages rather than files a ticket.

payload_or_id.name: Clients are served a stale value indefinitely after a write
payload_or_id.description: A key is read (caching it), then updated through admin.update_value. Storage holds the new value; the cache holds the old one and is never invalidated or expired, so get_value returns the superseded value for the remaining life of the process. The existing counter records every one of those reads as outcome=success -- the service cannot distinguish a correct read from a permanently wrong one. This is the last link of the invalidation chain, not the place to detect it.

payload_or_id.name: A newly written key never becomes visible to readers
payload_or_id.description: A key requested before it exists is cached as None, and that negative is never invalidated by the subsequent write nor expired by the evictor. get_value keeps returning None to the client long after the key is present and correct in storage. Distinct from fm-stale-value-served in symptom and in likely blast radius: a client polling for a key's creation is a common pattern, and it never terminates.

payload_or_id.name: Process is OOM-killed and drops all in-flight requests
payload_or_id.description: Unbounded cache growth eventually exhausts the process memory limit. The runtime OOM-kills it, taking every in-flight request with it and, worse, potentially interrupting a Storage.put mid-rewrite (see fm-nonatomic-full-file-rewrite). Because the cache is memory-resident only, the restart also wipes it -- so the symptom is a repeating crash-and-recover cycle whose period shortens as unique-key traffic rises.

payload_or_id.name: Reads fail outright with StorageError
payload_or_id.description: A storage read failure propagates through Cache.get and out of get_value to the client after incrementing outcome=error. This is the one failure mode the service already instruments, and it is also the least insidious -- it is loud, immediate, and attributable. Note it only fires for a cache miss: clients whose keys are already cached keep being served from memory, so the error rate understates the breakage.

payload_or_id.name: Most or all keys disappear from the store at once
payload_or_id.description: An interrupted or space-exhausted whole-file rewrite truncates the store. Because a missing file and a missing key both return None rather than raising, the surviving symptom is get_value returning None for keys that used to resolve -- counted as outcome=success. Mass data loss is therefore indistinguishable, in the current instrumentation, from clients simply asking for keys that do not exist.

payload_or_id.name: A write reported as successful is silently lost
payload_or_id.description: update_value returns without error while the key's value never reaches the durable store, because a concurrent put overwrote it from a stale in-memory snapshot. Readers see the pre-write value forever and the writer has no signal that anything went wrong. No read-back verification, no write counter, and no version or checksum exists to contradict the false success.

payload_or_id.name: A read returns another key's value
payload_or_id.description: Delimiter and newline handling in the flat file let one key's record alias onto another's, so get_value returns a well-formed but wrong value belonging to a different key. This is the worst-behaved failure in the set: it is silent, it is counted as success, it may cross a tenant or user boundary, and unlike staleness the value was never correct for this key at any point in time.

payload_or_id.name: Every value served ages without limit because writes stopped
payload_or_id.description: With the only writer stopped or failing, reads keep succeeding and returning progressively older data across the whole keyspace. Severity is warning rather than critical because the service is still serving correct-as-of-last-sync values and the remedy is to restore the writer, not to intervene in the read path -- but the window before anyone notices is unbounded, since nothing measures data age.

payload_or_id.name: Read latency degrades as the store and cache grow
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss costs a full file read and linear scan, and every write costs a full read plus rewrite, so per-operation latency rises with total key count while memory pressure from the unbounded cache adds GC and swap cost. payload_or_id.title: Clients are served a stale value indefinitely after a write
payload_or_id.description: A key is read (caching it), then updated through admin.update_value. payload_or_id.title: A newly written key never becomes visible to readers

payload_or_id.title: Most or all keys disappear from the store at once

payload_or_id.title: A write reported as successful is silently lost

payload_or_id.title: A read returns another key's value

payload_or_id.description: With the only writer stopped or failing, reads keep succeeding and returning progressively older data across the whole keyspace. payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss costs a full file read and linear scan, and every write costs a full read plus rewrite, so per-operation latency rises with total key count while memory pressure from the unbounded cache adds GC and swap cost. Phase 2 accepted — 25 `failure_modes` entries: 9 user-visible ends, 16 upstream links.

**The chains, upstream → user-visible:**

```
evictor unit mismatch ┐
eviction not scheduled ┼─▶ cache never expires ──┬─▶ STALE VALUE SERVED (critical)
write skips invalidation ┘                        │
negative result cached ───────────────────────────┴─▶ NEW KEY NEVER VISIBLE (critical)

evictor unit mismatch ┬─▶ cache unbounded growth ──▶ PROCESS OOM-KILLED (critical)
eviction not scheduled ┘                         └──▶ READ LATENCY DEGRADES (warning)

filesystem unavailable ─┬─▶ storage read OSError ──▶ READ ERRORS TO CLIENTS (critical)
                        ├─▶ storage write OSError ─┬─▶ DATA GOES STALE GLOBALLY (warning)
                        │   └─▶ sync job stops ────┘
                        └─▶ non-atomic rewrite ────▶ MASS KEY LOSS (critical)

concurrent put lost update ──▶ ACKNOWLEDGED WRITE LOST (critical)
delimiter collision ┬────────▶ WRONG VALUE RETURNED (critical)
newline corruption  ┘
```

**Three judgements worth your attention:**

**1. The eviction bug has two independent causes, and I documented both.** The unit mismatch is the one the code comments admit to. But nothing in this repo calls `run_eviction_pass` at all — the scheduler is out of repo. Fixing the seconds/milliseconds arithmetic closes only half the chain; if the scheduler was never wired up, the cache still never expires and every downstream symptom is unchanged. A single "eviction is broken" entry would have hidden that, and the metric that detects one does not detect the other.

**2. Missing data and destroyed data are currently the same signal.** `Storage.get` returns `None` both when the file is absent and when the key isn't in it — only an `OSError` on an *existing* file raises. So a truncated store, a wiped volume, and a client asking for a key that never existed all produce `outcome="success"` with a `None` result. That is why `fm-mass-key-loss` is recorded as user-visible-critical despite the service reporting perfect health throughout.

**3. I found one failure mode the source comments don't mention.** `Storage.put` calls `write_text` directly on the live path — it truncates and rewrites the real file with no temp-file-and-rename. A crash mid-write (including an OOM kill from the *other* chain) destroys every key after the truncation point, not just the one being written. One failed write has a blast radius of the entire dataset, which is why it carries `critical` severity even though it is not itself user-visible.

**Coverage going into Phase 3:** 2 of 25 are alertable today — `fm-read-errors-surface-to-clients` (the existing `outcome="error"` label) and `fm-metrics-scrape-stops` (Prometheus' own scrape-health signal, needs no service change). 22 are metric gaps. 1 is excluded: `fm-metrics-not-exposed`, because a process cannot emit a metric announcing its own metrics are unreachable — it's a deploy-time wiring check, and its runtime form is covered by the scrape-health alert.

That exclusion is a caveat on everything below it: **no metric I recommend in Phase 3 is alertable until someone confirms the embedding process actually starts an exposition endpoint.** The repo creates a `Counter` and never serves it.

The run pauses here. Say when to start Phase 3 (metric coverage).

Phase 3 -- metric coverage: inventory the metrics this codebase actually implements as
Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure
mode's coverage status: `alertable` (implemented metrics suffice; only an alert rule is
missing), `metric-gap` (implemented metrics cannot detect it adequately; propose the
metric change needed), or `excluded` (record the reason). Every metric recommendation
must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a
change to an existing one. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 3.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Not alertable in principle from inside the service: a process cannot emit a metric announcing that its own metrics are unreachable, and no rule can distinguish 'never exposed' from 'exposed but silent' using the same missing signal. It is a deploy-time wiring precondition, verified once by confirming the embedding process starts an exposition endpoint, not a recurring runtime condition.
payload_or_id.rationale: Its runtime manifestation IS covered, by fm-metrics-scrape-stops. Kept in the artifact rather than dropped because every metric recommendation in this phase and every alert in phase 4 is void until this wiring is confirmed present -- the repo defines a Counter and never serves it.

Nothing implemented observes the evictor at all: run_eviction_pass returns its count and every caller discards it. The bug's signature -- passes executing while evictions stay pinned at zero and entry count climbs -- needs the evicted counter and the pass counter together, since either alone is ambiguous between this and fm-eviction-not-scheduled.

No implemented metric can see whether an out-of-repo scheduler is calling the pass. The last-run timestamp gauge is the load-bearing one: absence of runs produces no errors, no exceptions, and no change in any existing series, so only a signal that ages on its own can distinguish 'not scheduled' from 'scheduled and healthy'.

process_resident_memory_bytes shows memory rising but not why, and cannot separate cache growth from any other leak or from legitimate load. Entry count is the attributing signal, and it is the earliest point in the whole chain at which the eviction defect becomes visible -- within one TTL period rather than whenever the container limit happens to be reached.

A negative hit is indistinguishable from a real hit in every implemented signal: both return from cache, both increment outcome=success. The result label with a distinct negative_hit value is the only way to count them, and the code already computes the distinction it currently discards.

The write path emits nothing whatsoever, so the absence of an invalidation call is unobservable. Instrumenting Cache.evict makes the defect visible as a divergence rather than requiring the bug to be fixed first: writes climb while invalidations sourced from writes stay permanently absent.

The existing counter records a stale read and a correct read identically as outcome=success -- it cannot tell the difference in principle, since staleness is a property of the value, not of the call. Detection must therefore happen upstream: at the missing invalidation, and at the age of the oldest surviving entry, which bounds how stale any served value can be.

Returning None for a key that exists in storage is currently counted as a success with no distinguishing feature at all. Splitting not_found out of success makes the symptom countable, and the negative_hit label identifies the specific mechanism, letting an alert fire on cached negatives rather than on legitimate misses.

Partially covered: the request counter's error label reflects read failures, but only those reaching a cache miss, and it cannot separate a read failure from any other StorageError source. Counting at the OSError handler in storage.py attributes the failure to the read operation itself, one hop closer to the cause and independent of cache behaviour.

Write failures are invisible in every implemented metric -- the error is raised past an uninstrumented update_value into an out-of-repo caller. Reads keep succeeding from the last good file throughout, so the service's only current signal stays green while it has entirely stopped accepting data.

The service never samples free space or mount state, so this root cause is only ever inferred after an operation has already failed. Free-space trend is the single earliest predictive signal in this analysis -- hours of warning before the failure it causes -- and may already exist on the host via node_exporter, which should be checked before adding a service-level gauge.

A truncated store is well-formed and parses cleanly, so no error path is taken and nothing implemented can see it. Key count is the detector after the fact -- it cannot legitimately decrease in a design with no delete -- and free space is the detector before it. Note that metrics can only observe this failure; removing it requires a temp-file-and-rename in storage.py.

The most dangerous blind spot in the service: because a missing file and a missing key both return None rather than raising, total data loss is recorded as unbroken success. Three independent signals are proposed because the consequence is severe and each fails differently -- key count catches the drop, file presence catches a wiped volume, and the not_found split catches the client-visible effect.

Both writers succeed, nothing raises, and the resulting file is valid, so no passive metric can observe the loss -- only an active read-back check can. Flagged as the weakest coverage proposed here: the check doubles write I/O and is itself racy. Where write volume makes that unacceptable, the honest position is that this stays uncovered and is fixed by locking instead.

Inherits its coverage entirely from the upstream lost-update entry: a write that was acknowledged but never landed produces no signal anywhere, in any layer, at any time. Read-back verification is the only mechanism that can contradict the false success, with the cost and raciness caveats recorded there.

The collision produces a well-formed record, so parsing succeeds and no implemented signal moves. Validating the key for a delimiter at write time counts the defect at the moment it enters the store, which is the only point where it is cheap to see and before any client has been served a wrong value.

Same mechanism, opposite side of the record: an embedded newline splits one entry into two on the next read, silently injecting a phantom key. Nothing implemented parses defensively or counts malformed lines, so the corruption is invisible until a client is served the wrong value.

Unobservable at the read path by construction -- the service has no way to know the value it returned belongs to another key, and the request counter records it as a success. Detection must sit at the write and parse boundaries where the aliasing is created, which is why the anomaly counter serves this user-visible failure through its two upstream causes rather than directly.

A stopped writer produces silence, and silence is the one thing rate-based alerting cannot distinguish from health. Time-since-last-successful-write is the only proposed signal that rises on its own without cooperation from the failed component, which is what makes it able to detect absence rather than error.

Reads succeed throughout and the existing counter stays perfectly flat and green while every value served ages without limit. Nothing in the service measures data age, so the detection point is the writer's silence, not the reader's behaviour.

Neither file size nor operation cost is measured anywhere. Both matter because the design is O(file size) on every read and every write, so the growth curve is a leading indicator of the latency degradation that eventually reaches users, with lead time proportional to how early the trend is watched.

No timing instrumentation exists at any layer -- the counter records the same successes however slow they become. Storage-operation latency is the direct measure, while key count and cache size explain which of the two growth curves is driving it, which is what makes the alert actionable rather than merely true.

event.text:
Phase 3 accepted: 2 metrics inventoried, 17 recommendations, all 25 coverage statuses set.

**What's actually implemented.** One hand-written metric, `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`, defined at `api.py:19-23` with exactly two emission sites (`:30` error, `:32` success). No Gauge, Histogram or Summary anywhere; no `/metrics` endpoint in the repo.

I also recorded a second entry you should know about: importing `prometheus_client` auto-registers its `ProcessCollector` into the default registry, so `process_resident_memory_bytes`, `process_start_time_seconds` and friends are already available on the same scrape without anyone writing them. That's Linux-only — the collector no-ops where `/proc` is absent.

**Coverage: 3 alertable, 21 metric-gap, 1 excluded.**

The process collector changed one verdict. `fm-process-oom-kill` is **alertable today** — rising RSS then a jump in start time is a detectable crash-and-restart, no code change needed. But I want to be explicit that this is weak comfort: it detects the crash. The upstream `fm-cache-unbounded-growth` stays a metric-gap, and that's where the five minutes of warning actually live.

**Three judgements worth your attention:**

**1. One recommendation is a change, not an addition.** `mr-get-value-outcome-not-found` splits `not_found` out of `success` on the existing counter. Today a truncated store and a client asking for keys that don't exist produce byte-identical telemetry. It's a compatible extension — rules on `outcome="error"` keep working — but any dashboard treating `success` as total requests will drop by the not-found share.

**2. Two metrics detect their bug without the bug being fixed first.** `mr-cache-invalidations` instruments `Cache.evict` with a `source` label; because no writer calls it, `source="write"` stays permanently absent while `kvstore_writes_total` climbs. That divergence *is* the defect, expressed as data. Same trick for the evictor: passes running while evictions stay pinned at zero. Both keep earning their place afterwards as regression guards.

**3. I flagged my own weakest proposal.** `mr-write-verify-failures` (read back after write) is the only way to see a lost update — both writers succeed, nothing raises, the file stays valid. But it doubles write I/O and is racy in exactly the case it detects. If write volume makes that unacceptable, the honest position is that `fm-acknowledged-write-lost` stays uncovered and gets fixed with locking or an atomic rename instead of watched. I'd rather say that than record coverage that won't survive contact with a review.

**The caveat over everything:** `fm-metrics-not-exposed` is the one exclusion. A process cannot emit a metric announcing its own metrics are unreachable. Every recommendation above is void until someone confirms the embedding process serves an exposition endpoint — the repo defines a `Counter` and never serves it.

Also worth noting: three failure modes can be *observed* but not *fixed* by metrics — `fm-nonatomic-full-file-rewrite`, `fm-concurrent-put-lost-update`, and the delimiter pair. A temp-file-and-rename in `storage.py` would remove the first two outright. Alerting on them is second best.

The run pauses here. Say when to start Phase 4 (alert recommendations).

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert
serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode
may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).
Phase 4. Probing the alert schema with the one rule that's deployable today.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreMetricsScrapeDown
payload_or_id.title: Kvstore metrics stopped being scraped

annotations.summary: Kvstore is not being scraped -- every other kvstore alert is blind
annotations.description: The kvstore scrape target is down or has disappeared from service discovery. This alert must exist before any other rule here is trusted: every other kvstore alert is a threshold over a metric this service emits, and absence of data satisfies none of them, so a scrape failure silently disables the entire alert set while looking exactly like health. The absent() arm covers the target vanishing from discovery entirely, which up{} alone cannot express. Pages rather than ticketing because the blindness window is the time during which any other failure here goes undetected. Deployable today with no code change -- it uses the scrape-health series Prometheus generates about its own targets, not anything kvstore emits.

event.text: Schema confirmed. Submitting the remaining 20 rules.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreReadErrorRate
payload_or_id.title: get_value is returning errors to clients

annotations.summary: Over 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: Reads are failing outright and the error is reaching clients. This is the only alert in the set that works today with no code change. Two limits to remember while responding: the counter only moves for requests that reach a cache miss, so clients holding cached keys keep succeeding and the true breakage is worse than the ratio suggests; and a low absolute request rate makes this ratio jumpy, so pair it with the storage-level alert rather than treating a quiet period as evidence of health.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageReadErrors
payload_or_id.title: Backing file read failures

annotations.summary: Storage read operations are raising OSError
annotations.description: Counted at the OSError handler in storage.py, one hop closer to the cause than the request counter and independent of whether a cache hit spared the client. Fires earlier and more reliably than KvstoreReadErrorRate during a partial outage, because it does not depend on traffic reaching a cache miss. Investigate file permissions, the mount, and file-descriptor limits before assuming the fault is in kvstore itself.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWriteFailures
payload_or_id.title: Writes to the backing store are failing

annotations.summary: Storage writes are failing -- the store has stopped accepting new data
annotations.description: Nothing on the read path can detect this: reads keep succeeding against the last good file, so the service looks entirely healthy while it silently stops accepting data. Both arms are included because they fail independently -- the write counter sees failures at the admin entrypoint, the storage counter sees them at the OSError handler, and a write path added later that bypasses admin.update_value would only be caught by the second. Check free space first; a full disk here also risks the whole-store truncation covered by KvstoreStoreKeysDropped.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded
payload_or_id.title: Cache is growing with no evictions

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is rising and nothing has been evicted for 6 hours
annotations.description: The earliest detectable point in the chain that ends in an OOM kill, and the conjunction is what makes it specific: a growing cache is normal during warm-up, and zero evictions is normal on an idle service, but together over six hours they mean eviction is not working. Distinguishing which cause -- broken arithmetic or an absent scheduler -- is what KvstoreEvictionEvictingNothing and KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning are for. Six hours rather than minutes because this is a slow failure and a shorter window would fire on ordinary traffic bursts.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreResidentMemoryGrowing
payload_or_id.title: Process memory trending toward the limit

annotations.summary: Kvstore RSS is on track to exceed its memory limit within 24 hours
annotations.description: The today-deployable stand-in for KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded: it uses process_resident_memory_bytes, which prometheus_client registers automatically, so it needs no code change at all. It is strictly worse than the cache-entries version -- it cannot attribute the growth to the cache rather than to any other leak, and it is Linux-only because the collector needs /proc. Replace the 2e9 threshold with the actual container memory limit; a prediction horizon shorter than the deploy-and-restart cycle will simply never fire.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is not being invoked

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed in 15 minutes
annotations.description: Detects the out-of-repo scheduler failing to call run_eviction_pass at all -- a failure that produces no errors and no change in any other series, because nothing happening looks exactly like nothing being wrong. The absent() arm matters as much as the threshold: it catches the case where the pass has never run once since startup, which the subtraction alone cannot express. Fifteen minutes is three times the 300s TTL, so it tolerates one or two missed cycles without flapping.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionEvictingNothing
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass runs but evicts nothing

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are executing but removing zero entries despite entries older than the TTL
annotations.description: This is the signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds comparison in evictor.py: the pass runs on schedule, walks every entry, and finds nothing expired because now - inserted_at_ms is always negative. The third clause is what makes it a defect rather than an idle service -- entries older than twice the TTL exist and were not removed. Fix is in evictor.py, and this alert is also the confirmation that the fix worked; the counter should start moving immediately after deploy.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheEntriesOutliveTTL
payload_or_id.title: Cached entries are far older than the TTL

annotations.summary: Oldest cache entry exceeds 3x TTL -- clients may be served values that old
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-stale-value-served: this number is a direct upper bound on how stale any value handed to a client can be, which no other signal in the service expresses. It fires under either eviction cause, which makes it the catch-all backstop for that chain -- deliberately overlapping the two more specific eviction alerts, because those diagnose while this one measures user impact. It also stays valid on a low-traffic keyspace where entry count looks stable while every entry is ancient.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWritesNotInvalidatingCache
payload_or_id.title: Writes are landing without invalidating the cache

annotations.summary: Successful writes are occurring but no cache invalidation is being recorded
annotations.description: Expresses the defect as a divergence between two series, so it fires against the current unfixed code rather than requiring the fix first: admin.update_value calls storage.put and never cache.evict, so the write-sourced invalidation series stays permanently empty while writes climb. The absent() arm is the one that fires today, since the series will not exist at all until Cache.evict is instrumented. After the fix this becomes the regression guard that catches any future write path added without an invalidation call.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNegativeCacheHits
payload_or_id.title: Clients are being served cached negative results

annotations.summary: Over 5% of cache lookups are returning a permanently cached None
annotations.description: A key read before it was first written is pinned to None in the cache and, with eviction broken, never re-checked against storage -- so a client polling for a key's creation never sees it appear. This ratio is the only way to distinguish that from legitimate misses, since both return None and both count as success at the API. A steady non-zero rate is the signature; a spike usually means a new caller is polling for keys ahead of the sync job that creates them.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreProcessRestarted
payload_or_id.title: Kvstore process restarted

annotations.summary: Kvstore restarted in the last hour -- in-flight requests were dropped
annotations.description: Deployable today with no code change. Catches the OOM kill at the end of the cache-growth chain, and a restart is doubly serious here: an interrupted Storage.put leaves the whole store truncated, so check KvstoreStoreKeysDropped immediately after this fires. Treat this as the failure of last resort rather than the detection point -- KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded should have fired hours earlier, and if it did not, the gap between the two is the thing to fix.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreKeysDropped
payload_or_id.title: Stored key count fell

annotations.summary: The number of keys in the store decreased -- data has been lost
annotations.description: Storage has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any fall is proof of data loss rather than a tuned threshold. The usual cause is an interrupted or space-exhausted whole-file rewrite in Storage.put, which truncates the file and destroys every key past the truncation point. Respond by restoring from backup, not by restarting: the process will come back healthy and serve the truncated store indefinitely without complaint.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFileMissing
payload_or_id.title: Backing store file is absent

annotations.summary: The backing store file does not exist -- every read returns not-found
annotations.description: Storage.get treats an absent file as an empty store and returns None rather than raising, so a wiped or unmounted volume produces zero errors and reads as perfect health. This alert exists because that silence is indistinguishable from a store nobody is querying. Check the mount before assuming deletion -- an unmounted volume presents identically, and restarting onto it will create a fresh empty file that makes the loss permanent.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNotFoundRatioSpike
payload_or_id.title: Not-found rate jumped against its own baseline

annotations.summary: Share of not-found reads has doubled against the same window yesterday
annotations.description: The client-visible companion to KvstoreStoreKeysDropped, and the one that catches data loss the writer never observes -- keys destroyed while no put is running leave the key-count gauge untouched until the next write. Compared against a day-ago baseline rather than a fixed threshold because the healthy not-found share is entirely workload-dependent and no absolute number generalises. The absolute-rate clause suppresses the ratio noise that a near-zero baseline would otherwise produce. Requires the not_found split from mr-get-value-outcome-not-found; without it, every one of these reads is recorded as a success.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNoRecentWrites
payload_or_id.title: No successful write in over an hour

annotations.summary: The data-sync job has not written successfully for over an hour
annotations.description: A stopped writer produces silence, and no rate-based rule can distinguish silence from health -- zero errors is what both look like. This is the one alert here driven by a signal that rises on its own without cooperation from the component that failed, which is exactly why it can detect absence. Set the threshold from the sync job's actual period; one hour is a placeholder, and a threshold shorter than the real interval will page on every normal quiet gap. Warning rather than critical because the service is still serving correct-as-of-last-sync data.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreRecordAnomalies
payload_or_id.title: Malformed records in the backing store

annotations.summary: A key containing a comma, a value containing a newline, or a duplicate/undelimited record was seen
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-wrong-value-returned: these anomalies make one key's record alias onto another's, so a read returns a well-formed value belonging to a different key -- potentially across a tenant boundary -- and is counted as a success. Any non-zero rate is a defect by definition, so no threshold tuning is needed. The kind label says which hazard fired: delimiter_in_key and newline_in_value are caught at write time before corruption enters the store, missing_delimiter and duplicate_key are found at read time and mean it is already there.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWriteVerifyFailures
payload_or_id.title: A write did not survive read-back

annotations.summary: A value written successfully was not present when read back
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file, so two overlapping writes each read the pre-existing state and the later one discards the earlier one's key. Both callers see success. Two caveats when this fires: a third write landing between the put and the read-back produces a false positive, so a single isolated firing under concurrent load may be the detector rather than the defect; and the underlying race is better removed by locking or an atomic temp-file rename than watched, in which case this alert and its metric should be retired rather than tuned.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageLatencyHigh
payload_or_id.title: Storage operation latency is high

annotations.summary: p99 storage operation latency above 500ms
annotations.description: Every get is a full file read plus linear scan and every put is a full read plus rewrite, so latency is the direct measure of this design meeting its scaling limit. Kept by operation because get and put degrade at different rates and the put tail moves first. The tail matters more than the mean here: large-file cost shows in p99 well before the average shifts. Set the 500ms threshold from the actual client timeout -- it is a placeholder, not a measured value.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFileGrowthProjection
payload_or_id.title: Backing file projected to reach an unworkable size

annotations.summary: Store file projected to exceed 1GB within a week at current growth
annotations.description: The store has no delete operation and is rewritten whole on every write, so its size only rises and per-operation cost rises with it. This is the leading indicator for KvstoreStorageLatencyHigh: it fires while there is still time to change the storage design, rather than once users are already feeling the latency. A week's horizon is chosen to be longer than the lead time any such change needs. Tune the 1GB threshold to the point where a full rewrite stops fitting comfortably in the write path's time budget.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFilesystemSpaceLow
payload_or_id.title: Store volume low or predicted to fill

annotations.summary: Store volume under 10% free or predicted full within 4 hours
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-nonatomic-full-file-rewrite: Storage.put truncates and rewrites the live file with no temp-file-and-rename, so running out of space mid-write destroys the entire dataset, not just the key being written. That consequence is what justifies paging on a disk that is merely trending full. This is the earliest signal in the whole analysis -- hours of warning, where everything else fires at or after the failure. Adjust the mountpoint label to the real store path, and confirm node_exporter covers that filesystem before relying on it; if it does not, the fallback service-level gauge from mr-filesystem-free-bytes is needed instead.

payload_or_id.name: prometheus_client registry and scrape path
payload_or_id.description: prometheus_client 0.26.0 and the scrape path that reads its default registry. Holds more than the service's own instrumentation: importing prometheus_client auto-registers ProcessCollector and PlatformCollector into the same default REGISTRY, so process_resident_memory_bytes, process_start_time_seconds, process_cpu_seconds_total and process_open_fds are exposed alongside the one hand-written counter without any code in this repo declaring them. It matters because it is the sole reason any alert is deployable against this service today. No HTTP exposition endpoint (start_http_server or equivalent) is created anywhere in this repo, so the registry has no confirmed sink: every metric here, hand-written or automatic, depends on the embedding process serving one.

payload_or_id.name: Flat-file backing store (storage.py)
payload_or_id.description: Backing key-value store (storage.Storage): a single delimited flat text file, one 'key,value' pair per line, read and rewritten in full on every operation. get() scans every line and returns the first key match, or None if the file is absent or the key is not found. put() reads the whole file into a dict, sets the key, mkdir -p's the parent, and rewrites the whole file. Three properties of that design drive most of this service's failure surface. The rewrite is non-atomic: write_text truncates and rewrites the live path with no temp-file-and-rename, so an interrupted write destroys every key past the truncation point. The read-modify-write is unsynchronised: no lock and no compare-and-swap, so overlapping writes silently discard each other and a concurrent read can observe a half-written file. And the serialisation has no escaping or quoting: a comma in a key aliases it onto another key, and a newline in a value splits one record into two. OSError is wrapped as StorageError; nothing else is signalled. Uninstrumented: no operation counter, no latency, no file-size or key-count metric.

payload_or_id.name: Filesystem holding the store file
payload_or_id.description: The local filesystem and the flat file path Storage was constructed with. Supplies durability, capacity, and permissions for every read and write. Its failures surface only as OSError -> StorageError, and the service itself never samples free space or mount state. Free space on this volume is nonetheless the earliest predictive signal available anywhere in this system -- it trends hours before the failure it causes, where every other signal fires at or after the event -- and it is the precondition for the most destructive outcome, since exhausting space mid-rewrite destroys the whole dataset rather than one key. Coverage may already exist outside this codebase: a host node_exporter reporting node_filesystem_avail_bytes for this mountpoint would cover it entirely, and whether one is present decides if a service-level gauge is needed at all.

payload_or_id.name: Process runtime and memory limit (container/host)
payload_or_id.description: The container or host runtime the service executes in, and the memory limit it enforces. It is the actor that terminates the process when the unbounded cache exhausts that limit, and that restarts it afterwards -- wiping the in-memory cache and, if a Storage.put was in flight, potentially leaving the store truncated. It also owns the CPU and file-descriptor budgets that bound every operation. Added after the fact: the original map had no component for it, which left the cache-growth chain ending at an actor the map did not contain, and gave the automatically-collected process_* metrics no component to attach to beyond the metrics registry. Its limit is the threshold that decides when growth becomes an outage, and that value lives in deployment configuration outside this repo.

payload_or_id.name: In-memory cache (cache.py)
payload_or_id.description: In-process, in-memory cache (cache.Cache) sitting in front of Storage, holding key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms). Cache.get consults its own dict first and only falls back to storage on a miss; it never re-checks storage for an already-cached key and never expires anything itself. Negative lookups are cached too (value=None is stored as an entry, and the hit check tests the Entry rather than the value, so a cached None is served as a hit). Expiry and size bounding are delegated entirely to the eviction pass, and Cache.evict exists for a writer to call after updating storage but no writer does. Memory is the resource it consumes without bound, which is why it depends on the process runtime that limits it. Uninstrumented: no hit/miss counter, no entry-count gauge, no age distribution.

Amendment applied and closed. The map is now 10 components.

**What changed, and why each was a real correction rather than polish:**

**1. `sm-prometheus-registry` was factually wrong.** Phase 1 said it "holds the service's one metric." It doesn't — importing `prometheus_client` auto-registers `ProcessCollector`, so `process_resident_memory_bytes` and `process_start_time_seconds` sit in the same registry with nothing in this repo declaring them. That's not trivia: it's the entire reason two Phase 4 alerts are deployable today. A map that undercounts what's available with no code change leads whoever reads it to build instrumentation they already have. (Linux-only — the collector needs `/proc`.)

**2. `sm-storage-layer` omitted the properties that generate the failures.** The map described the full-file rewrite pattern but not that the rewrite is non-atomic, the read-modify-write is unsynchronised, and the serialisation has no escaping. Those three facts produced five failure modes between them. Someone reading only the map would see "rewrites the file" and not understand why a crash costs the whole dataset.

**3. `sm-backing-file-fs` understated what's possible.** Saying capacity "is not observed by anything in the service" is true but reads as though nothing can observe it. A host `node_exporter` would cover it entirely — and whether one exists decides if `mr-filesystem-free-bytes` needs writing at all.

**4. A component was missing.** Nothing in the map represented the process runtime and its memory limit. That left the cache-growth chain terminating in an actor the map didn't contain: the thing that enforces the limit, kills the process, and restarts it. `sm-cache-layer` now depends on it, memory being the resource it consumes without bound.

**One thing I deliberately did not do.** Adding `sm-process-runtime` arguably means `fm-process-oom-kill` should be re-attributed to it from `sm-cache-layer`. I left it — that's a Phase 2 edit, and the current attribution is defensible, since the cache is what consumes the memory even though the runtime is what enforces the limit. Folding a second phase's change into a map revision without asking seemed like the wrong call. Say so if you want it moved.

Worth noting what this exercise says about the process generally: the map got better because it was written *before* the failure analysis and revised *after*. The Phase 1 version was not wrong to write — it was the thing that made Phases 2–4 possible. But a system map written before you know how a system fails will always understate the parts that matter, and the revision pass is where that gets corrected. The registry error in particular would have propagated silently into "we need to add memory metrics" when they were already there.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreMetricsScrapeDown
payload_or_id.title: Kvstore metrics stopped being scraped

annotations.summary: Kvstore is not being scraped -- every other kvstore alert is blind
annotations.description: The kvstore scrape target is down or has disappeared from service discovery. This alert must exist before any other rule here is trusted: every other kvstore alert is a threshold over a metric this service emits, and absence of data satisfies none of them, so a scrape failure silently disables the entire alert set while looking exactly like health. The absent() arm covers the target vanishing from discovery entirely, which up{} alone cannot express. Pages rather than ticketing because the blindness window is the time during which any other failure here goes undetected. Deployable today with no code change -- it uses the scrape-health series Prometheus generates about its own targets, not anything kvstore emits.

event.text: Key confirmed. Repairing the remaining 20.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreReadErrorRate
payload_or_id.title: get_value is returning errors to clients

annotations.summary: Over 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: Reads are failing outright and the error is reaching clients. This is the only alert in the set that works today with no code change. Two limits to remember while responding: the counter only moves for requests that reach a cache miss, so clients holding cached keys keep succeeding and the true breakage is worse than the ratio suggests; and a low absolute request rate makes this ratio jumpy, so pair it with the storage-level alert rather than treating a quiet period as evidence of health.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageReadErrors
payload_or_id.title: Backing file read failures

annotations.summary: Storage read operations are raising OSError
annotations.description: Counted at the OSError handler in storage.py, one hop closer to the cause than the request counter and independent of whether a cache hit spared the client. Fires earlier and more reliably than KvstoreReadErrorRate during a partial outage, because it does not depend on traffic reaching a cache miss. Investigate file permissions, the mount, and file-descriptor limits before assuming the fault is in kvstore itself.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWriteFailures
payload_or_id.title: Writes to the backing store are failing

annotations.summary: Storage writes are failing -- the store has stopped accepting new data
annotations.description: Nothing on the read path can detect this: reads keep succeeding against the last good file, so the service looks entirely healthy while it silently stops accepting data. Both arms are included because they fail independently -- the write counter sees failures at the admin entrypoint, the storage counter sees them at the OSError handler, and a write path added later that bypasses admin.update_value would only be caught by the second. Check free space first; a full disk here also risks the whole-store truncation covered by KvstoreStoreKeysDropped.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded
payload_or_id.title: Cache is growing with no evictions

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is rising and nothing has been evicted for 6 hours
annotations.description: The earliest detectable point in the chain that ends in an OOM kill, and the conjunction is what makes it specific: a growing cache is normal during warm-up, and zero evictions is normal on an idle service, but together over six hours they mean eviction is not working. Distinguishing which cause -- broken arithmetic or an absent scheduler -- is what KvstoreEvictionEvictingNothing and KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning are for. Six hours rather than minutes because this is a slow failure and a shorter window would fire on ordinary traffic bursts.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreResidentMemoryGrowing
payload_or_id.title: Process memory trending toward the limit

annotations.summary: Kvstore RSS is on track to exceed its memory limit within 24 hours
annotations.description: The today-deployable stand-in for KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded: it uses process_resident_memory_bytes, which prometheus_client registers automatically, so it needs no code change at all. It is strictly worse than the cache-entries version -- it cannot attribute the growth to the cache rather than to any other leak, and it is Linux-only because the collector needs /proc. Replace the 2e9 threshold with the actual container memory limit; a prediction horizon shorter than the deploy-and-restart cycle will simply never fire.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is not being invoked

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed in 15 minutes
annotations.description: Detects the out-of-repo scheduler failing to call run_eviction_pass at all -- a failure that produces no errors and no change in any other series, because nothing happening looks exactly like nothing being wrong. The absent() arm matters as much as the threshold: it catches the case where the pass has never run once since startup, which the subtraction alone cannot express. Fifteen minutes is three times the 300s TTL, so it tolerates one or two missed cycles without flapping.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionEvictingNothing
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass runs but evicts nothing

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are executing but removing zero entries despite entries older than the TTL
annotations.description: This is the signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds comparison in evictor.py: the pass runs on schedule, walks every entry, and finds nothing expired because now - inserted_at_ms is always negative. The third clause is what makes it a defect rather than an idle service -- entries older than twice the TTL exist and were not removed. Fix is in evictor.py, and this alert is also the confirmation that the fix worked; the counter should start moving immediately after deploy.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheEntriesOutliveTTL
payload_or_id.title: Cached entries are far older than the TTL

annotations.summary: Oldest cache entry exceeds 3x TTL -- clients may be served values that old
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-stale-value-served: this number is a direct upper bound on how stale any value handed to a client can be, which no other signal in the service expresses. It fires under either eviction cause, which makes it the catch-all backstop for that chain -- deliberately overlapping the two more specific eviction alerts, because those diagnose while this one measures user impact. It also stays valid on a low-traffic keyspace where entry count looks stable while every entry is ancient.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWritesNotInvalidatingCache
payload_or_id.title: Writes are landing without invalidating the cache

annotations.summary: Successful writes are occurring but no cache invalidation is being recorded
annotations.description: Expresses the defect as a divergence between two series, so it fires against the current unfixed code rather than requiring the fix first: admin.update_value calls storage.put and never cache.evict, so the write-sourced invalidation series stays permanently empty while writes climb. The absent() arm is the one that fires today, since the series will not exist at all until Cache.evict is instrumented. After the fix this becomes the regression guard that catches any future write path added without an invalidation call.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNegativeCacheHits
payload_or_id.title: Clients are being served cached negative results

annotations.summary: Over 5% of cache lookups are returning a permanently cached None
annotations.description: A key read before it was first written is pinned to None in the cache and, with eviction broken, never re-checked against storage -- so a client polling for a key's creation never sees it appear. This ratio is the only way to distinguish that from legitimate misses, since both return None and both count as success at the API. A steady non-zero rate is the signature; a spike usually means a new caller is polling for keys ahead of the sync job that creates them.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreProcessRestarted
payload_or_id.title: Kvstore process restarted

annotations.summary: Kvstore restarted in the last hour -- in-flight requests were dropped
annotations.description: Deployable today with no code change. Catches the OOM kill at the end of the cache-growth chain, and a restart is doubly serious here: an interrupted Storage.put leaves the whole store truncated, so check KvstoreStoreKeysDropped immediately after this fires. Treat this as the failure of last resort rather than the detection point -- KvstoreCacheGrowingUnbounded should have fired hours earlier, and if it did not, the gap between the two is the thing to fix.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreKeysDropped
payload_or_id.title: Stored key count fell

annotations.summary: The number of keys in the store decreased -- data has been lost
annotations.description: Storage has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any fall is proof of data loss rather than a tuned threshold. The usual cause is an interrupted or space-exhausted whole-file rewrite in Storage.put, which truncates the file and destroys every key past the truncation point. Respond by restoring from backup, not by restarting: the process will come back healthy and serve the truncated store indefinitely without complaint.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFileMissing
payload_or_id.title: Backing store file is absent

annotations.summary: The backing store file does not exist -- every read returns not-found
annotations.description: Storage.get treats an absent file as an empty store and returns None rather than raising, so a wiped or unmounted volume produces zero errors and reads as perfect health. This alert exists because that silence is indistinguishable from a store nobody is querying. Check the mount before assuming deletion -- an unmounted volume presents identically, and restarting onto it will create a fresh empty file that makes the loss permanent.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNotFoundRatioSpike
payload_or_id.title: Not-found rate jumped against its own baseline

annotations.summary: Share of not-found reads has doubled against the same window yesterday
annotations.description: The client-visible companion to KvstoreStoreKeysDropped, and the one that catches data loss the writer never observes -- keys destroyed while no put is running leave the key-count gauge untouched until the next write. Compared against a day-ago baseline rather than a fixed threshold because the healthy not-found share is entirely workload-dependent and no absolute number generalises. The absolute-rate clause suppresses the ratio noise that a near-zero baseline would otherwise produce. Requires the not_found split from mr-get-value-outcome-not-found; without it, every one of these reads is recorded as a success.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNoRecentWrites
payload_or_id.title: No successful write in over an hour

annotations.summary: The data-sync job has not written successfully for over an hour
annotations.description: A stopped writer produces silence, and no rate-based rule can distinguish silence from health -- zero errors is what both look like. This is the one alert here driven by a signal that rises on its own without cooperation from the component that failed, which is exactly why it can detect absence. Set the threshold from the sync job's actual period; one hour is a placeholder, and a threshold shorter than the real interval will page on every normal quiet gap. Warning rather than critical because the service is still serving correct-as-of-last-sync data.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreRecordAnomalies
payload_or_id.title: Malformed records in the backing store

annotations.summary: A key containing a comma, a value containing a newline, or a duplicate/undelimited record was seen
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-wrong-value-returned: these anomalies make one key's record alias onto another's, so a read returns a well-formed value belonging to a different key -- potentially across a tenant boundary -- and is counted as a success. Any non-zero rate is a defect by definition, so no threshold tuning is needed. The kind label says which hazard fired: delimiter_in_key and newline_in_value are caught at write time before corruption enters the store, missing_delimiter and duplicate_key are found at read time and mean it is already there.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWriteVerifyFailures
payload_or_id.title: A write did not survive read-back

annotations.summary: A value written successfully was not present when read back
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file, so two overlapping writes each read the pre-existing state and the later one discards the earlier one's key. Both callers see success. Two caveats when this fires: a third write landing between the put and the read-back produces a false positive, so a single isolated firing under concurrent load may be the detector rather than the defect; and the underlying race is better removed by locking or an atomic temp-file rename than watched, in which case this alert and its metric should be retired rather than tuned.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageLatencyHigh
payload_or_id.title: Storage operation latency is high

annotations.summary: p99 storage operation latency above 500ms
annotations.description: Every get is a full file read plus linear scan and every put is a full read plus rewrite, so latency is the direct measure of this design meeting its scaling limit. Kept by operation because get and put degrade at different rates and the put tail moves first. The tail matters more than the mean here: large-file cost shows in p99 well before the average shifts. Set the 500ms threshold from the actual client timeout -- it is a placeholder, not a measured value.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFileGrowthProjection
payload_or_id.title: Backing file projected to reach an unworkable size

annotations.summary: Store file projected to exceed 1GB within a week at current growth
annotations.description: The store has no delete operation and is rewritten whole on every write, so its size only rises and per-operation cost rises with it. This is the leading indicator for KvstoreStorageLatencyHigh: it fires while there is still time to change the storage design, rather than once users are already feeling the latency. A week's horizon is chosen to be longer than the lead time any such change needs. Tune the 1GB threshold to the point where a full rewrite stops fitting comfortably in the write path's time budget.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStoreFilesystemSpaceLow
payload_or_id.title: Store volume low or predicted to fill

annotations.summary: Store volume under 10% free or predicted full within 4 hours
annotations.description: Critical because it serves fm-nonatomic-full-file-rewrite: Storage.put truncates and rewrites the live file with no temp-file-and-rename, so running out of space mid-write destroys the entire dataset, not just the key being written. That consequence is what justifies paging on a disk that is merely trending full. This is the earliest signal in the whole analysis -- hours of warning, where everything else fires at or after the failure. Adjust the mountpoint label to the real store path, and confirm node_exporter covers that filesystem before relying on it; if it does not, the fallback service-level gauge from mr-filesystem-free-bytes is needed instead.

annotations.description: Every get is a full file read plus linear scan and every put is a full read plus rewrite, so latency is the direct measure of this design meeting its scaling limit. annotations.summary: Store file projected to exceed 1GB within a week at current growth
annotations.description: The store has no delete operation and is rewritten whole on every write, so its size only rises and per-operation cost rises with it. annotations.summary: Store volume under 10% free or predicted full within 4 hours
