payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass never expires anything (seconds vs milliseconds)
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.get sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS. The expired list is always empty, no entry is ever evicted, and the function always returns 0. The pass can run perfectly on schedule and still do nothing -- the only in-code signal it offers (the return count) reads identically to a healthy idle cache.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: No code in this repo calls run_eviction_pass; the scheduler that is supposed to drive it lives outside the service. If it is never wired up, is misconfigured, crashes, or has its interval set far longer than TTL_SECONDS, eviction simply does not happen. This is independent of fm-evictor-unit-mismatch and produces the same downstream effects, so fixing the unit bug alone does not close the chain.

payload_or_id.title: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value accepts a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put; it never calls cache.evict(key). Cache.get never re-checks storage for a key it already holds, so the cache and the backing store diverge the instant a write lands for any cached key. The divergence persists until eviction removes the entry -- which, given fm-evictor-unit-mismatch and fm-eviction-not-scheduled, is never.

payload_or_id.title: Missing-key result is cached as a permanent negative
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the storage result unconditionally, including None for a key that does not yet exist, and its hit check is `entry is not None` on the Entry rather than on the value. A key read before it is first written is pinned to None in the cache. Combined with the broken eviction, that negative is permanent for the process lifetime, so the key stays invisible no matter how many times it is later written.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get inserts an entry for every key it is asked about and nothing removes entries, so resident set grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Under sustained unique-key traffic -- including a scan, a scraper, or an attacker requesting random keys -- growth is bounded only by available memory. Nothing in the service reports the entry count, so the growth is invisible until the process dies.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file grows without bound and is rescanned in full
payload_or_id.description: Storage has no delete operation and put rewrites the entire file, so the file only ever grows. Every get does a full read_text plus a linear scan, and every put does a full read plus a full rewrite, making both O(file size). Cost per operation therefore rises continuously with key count. No metric records file size, line count, or operation latency.

payload_or_id.title: Filesystem full, unmounted, or permission-changed
payload_or_id.description: The volume holding the store file fills, is remounted read-only, is unmounted, or has its ownership changed. This is the shared root cause beneath both storage read and write failures and beneath the non-atomic rewrite hazard. Free space and mount state are external conditions that the service never samples, and they are detectable well before any operation actually fails.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file cannot be read
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get wraps OSError as StorageError: the file exists but is unreadable through lost permissions, a corrupt or unmounted filesystem, an exhausted file-descriptor limit, or an I/O error. Note the asymmetry -- an absent file is NOT an error here, it returns None, so a lost or wiped store reads as 'every key missing' rather than as a failure.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file cannot be written
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put wraps OSError as StorageError: disk full, read-only remount, lost permissions, or a failed parent mkdir. StorageError propagates to admin.update_value, which neither catches nor records it, and on to the out-of-repo sync job whose handling is unknown. Reads keep succeeding from the stale file throughout, so the service looks entirely healthy while it has stopped accepting new data.

payload_or_id.title: Whole-store rewrite is not atomic
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads every pair into a dict and then calls write_text on the live path, truncating the real file and rewriting it in place with no temp-file-and-rename. A crash, OOM kill, container eviction, or ENOSPC part-way through the write leaves the store truncated or half-written -- every key after the truncation point is destroyed, not just the one being written. The blast radius of one failed write is the entire dataset.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file with no lock and no compare-and-swap. Two overlapping puts each read the pre-existing state and the later writer's rewrite discards the earlier writer's key. A concurrent get can also observe the file mid-rewrite and read a truncated snapshot. Both puts return successfully, so the loss is entirely silent.

payload_or_id.title: Key containing the delimiter collides with another key
payload_or_id.description: Lines are split with partition(','), taking everything before the first comma as the key. A stored key containing a comma -- 'a,b' with value 'v' -- is written as the line 'a,b,v', which on read parses as key 'a' with value 'b,v'. A lookup of the unrelated key 'a' matches that line and returns 'b,v'. The store has no escaping or quoting, so key namespaces that permit commas silently alias onto each other.

payload_or_id.title: Newline in a value corrupts subsequent records
payload_or_id.description: Records are separated by newlines with no escaping, so a value containing a newline is written as two physical lines. On the next read the tail of that value is parsed as an independent record whose key is whatever precedes its first comma, injecting a phantom key and a corrupt value into the store. A single write of untrusted content can therefore create or overwrite arbitrary keys.

payload_or_id.title: Data-sync job stops running
payload_or_id.description: The out-of-repo periodic sync job is the only writer of new values. If it stops being scheduled, crashes, or fails every run against StorageError, the store simply stops receiving updates. Every read keeps succeeding and returning the last-synced value, so the service's one existing metric stays entirely green while the data it serves ages without limit.

payload_or_id.description: The package creates a Counter but never starts an exposition endpoint (no start_http_server, no ASGI/WSGI mount, no pushgateway call) anywhere in the repo. payload_or_id.description: The scrape path breaks in production -- endpoint down, target dropped from service discovery, network partition to Prometheus -- while the service keeps serving. Pages rather than files a ticket because it silently disables detection of every other failure here.

payload_or_id.title: Clients are served a stale value indefinitely after a write
payload_or_id.description: A key is read (caching it), then updated through admin.update_value. Storage holds the new value; the cache holds the old one and is never invalidated or expired, so get_value returns the superseded value for the remaining life of the process. The existing counter records every one of those reads as outcome=success -- the service cannot distinguish a correct read from a permanently wrong one. This is the last link of the invalidation chain, not the place to detect it.

payload_or_id.title: A newly written key never becomes visible to readers
payload_or_id.description: A key requested before it exists is cached as None, and that negative is never invalidated by the subsequent write nor expired by the evictor. get_value keeps returning None to the client long after the key is present and correct in storage. Distinct from fm-stale-value-served in symptom and in likely blast radius: a client polling for a key's creation is a common pattern, and it never terminates.

payload_or_id.title: Process is OOM-killed and drops all in-flight requests
payload_or_id.description: Unbounded cache growth eventually exhausts the process memory limit. The runtime OOM-kills it, taking every in-flight request with it and, worse, potentially interrupting a Storage.put mid-rewrite (see fm-nonatomic-full-file-rewrite). Because the cache is memory-resident only, the restart also wipes it -- so the symptom is a repeating crash-and-recover cycle whose period shortens as unique-key traffic rises. Coverage status is alertable rather than metric-gap: the prometheus_client default ProcessCollector already exposes process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds, which detect the kill and the restart with no code change. Early detection of the cause remains a gap on the upstream entry fm-cache-unbounded-growth.

payload_or_id.title: Reads fail outright with StorageError
payload_or_id.description: A storage read failure propagates through Cache.get and out of get_value to the client after incrementing outcome=error. This is the one failure mode the service already instruments, and it is also the least insidious -- it is loud, immediate, and attributable. Note it only fires for a cache miss: clients whose keys are already cached keep being served from memory, so the error rate understates the breakage.

payload_or_id.title: Most or all keys disappear from the store at once
payload_or_id.description: An interrupted or space-exhausted whole-file rewrite truncates the store. Because a missing file and a missing key both return None rather than raising, the surviving symptom is get_value returning None for keys that used to resolve -- counted as outcome=success. Mass data loss is therefore indistinguishable, in the current instrumentation, from clients simply asking for keys that do not exist.

payload_or_id.title: A write reported as successful is silently lost
payload_or_id.description: update_value returns without error while the key's value never reaches the durable store, because a concurrent put overwrote it from a stale in-memory snapshot. Readers see the pre-write value forever and the writer has no signal that anything went wrong. No read-back verification, no write counter, and no version or checksum exists to contradict the false success.

payload_or_id.title: A read returns another key's value
payload_or_id.description: Delimiter and newline handling in the flat file let one key's record alias onto another's, so get_value returns a well-formed but wrong value belonging to a different key. This is the worst-behaved failure in the set: it is silent, it is counted as success, it may cross a tenant or user boundary, and unlike staleness the value was never correct for this key at any point in time.

payload_or_id.title: Every value served ages without limit because writes stopped
payload_or_id.description: With the only writer stopped or failing, reads keep succeeding and returning progressively older data across the whole keyspace. Severity is warning rather than critical because the service is still serving correct-as-of-last-sync values and the remedy is to restore the writer, not to intervene in the read path -- but the window before anyone notices is unbounded, since nothing measures data age.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the store and cache grow
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss costs a full file read and linear scan, and every write costs a full read plus rewrite, so per-operation latency rises with total key count while memory pressure from the unbounded cache adds GC and swap cost. The degradation is gradual and has no threshold at which anything currently changes state -- the counter records the same successes, just more slowly.
